evidence.claim: A former gravel road connects forest, sandstone gorges and caves.
evidence.quote: The Hocking Hills region is a deeply dissected area of the Allegheny Plateau in Appalachian Ohio, primarily in Hocking County, that features cliffs, gorges, rock shelters, and waterfalls.

evidence.claim: A former gravel road connects forest, sandstone gorges and caves.
evidence.quote: Within the park are over 25 miles (40 km) of hiking trails, rock formations, waterfalls, and recess caves.

evidence.claim: The Hocking Hills Scenic Byway follows State Route 374 through the hills and around Hocking State Forest.
evidence.quote: This 26.4 mile byway follows State Route 374 through Ohio's scenic Hocking Hills and around Hocking State Forest.

evidence.claim: Blackhand sandstone forms the region’s high cliffs and narrow, deep gorges.
evidence.quote: The relatively dramatic topography in this area is due to the presence of Blackhand sandstone, a formation that erodes to form high cliffs and narrow, deep gorges.

evidence.claim: Ohio’s transportation department includes Hocking Hills among America’s Byways and highlights its deep gorges and caves.
evidence.quote: America’s Byway HCB Hocking Hills Scenic Byway

evidence.claim: Ohio’s transportation department includes Hocking Hills among America’s Byways and highlights its deep gorges and caves.
evidence.quote: have deep gorges and caves

evidence.claim: The forest landscape includes steep ridges, narrow valleys and exposed sandstone, with eastern hemlock among its native trees. Rock shelters and waterfalls are part of the terrain the road serves.
evidence.quote: The forest sits in the unglaciated Allegheny Plateau and features exposed Blackhand sandstone, steep ridges, and narrow valleys.

evidence.claim: with eastern hemlock among its native trees.
evidence.quote: Native trees include eastern hemlock, oaks, maples, hickories, and tulip poplar.

evidence.claim: Rock shelters and waterfalls are part of the terrain the road serves.
evidence.quote: The area features not only forests, but frequent bluffs, rock shelters and waterfalls, due to the Blackhand sandstone.

evidence.claim: Rock shelters and waterfalls are part of the terrain the road serves.
evidence.quote: The road serves Hocking State Forest as well as Hocking Hills State Park

evidence.claim: The numbered highway began with an unnumbered gravel road added to the state system in 1932; by 1934 it was SR 374.
evidence.quote: In 1932, an unnumbered gravel road was included into the state highway system between Mound Crossing at SR 180 (now the southernmost intersection on SR 374 with SR 180) and the road that is now SR 664 in rural Hocking County. By 1934, the route had been numbered SR 374.

evidence.claim: Extensions in 1938 carried it to SR 56 in the south and US 33 at Rockbridge in the north.
evidence.quote: In 1938, SR 374 was extended at both ends by taking over what was SR 664 between SR 56 and Cedar Grove at the south end and was routed along SR 180 between Mound Crossing and what was then SR 678, and then along SR 678 to Rockbridge at the intersection of US 33.

evidence.claim: During the same decade as the highway’s early expansion, Civilian Conservation Corps crews replanted trees and built trails in the forest.
evidence.quote: During the 1930s, the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) helped replant trees and build trails.

evidence.claim: A later change addressed the meeting of cars and walkers: a one-mile realignment near Old Man’s Cave opened by January 2013 to reduce conflicts with pedestrians.
evidence.quote: The realignment was needed to reduce the conflict between traffic on the road and pedestrians in the vicinity of the park. The one-mile-long (1.6 km) realignment opened by January 2013.

evidence.claim: a one-mile realignment near Old Man’s Cave opened by January 2013 to reduce conflicts with pedestrians.
evidence.quote: A slight realignment occurred in the area of the Old Man's Caves within Hocking Hills State Park (along the section concurrent with SR 664) between 2011 and 2013.

evidence.claim: Traveling south, begin near Rockbridge at US 33 and follow SR 374 through the state forest and state park to SR 56, east of South Bloomingville.
evidence.quote: Its southern terminus is over 4 miles (6.4 km) east of the unincorporated village of South Bloomingville at State Route 56, and its northern terminus is near the unincorporated village of Rockbridge at US 33, west of Logan. The road serves Hocking State Forest as well as Hocking Hills State Park

evidence.claim: The park’s separate hiking areas include Rock House, Old Man’s Cave and Ash Cave, with sandstone formations reached from trails.
evidence.quote: The state park contains several distinct landmarks that can be accessed from hiking trails.

evidence.claim: The park’s separate hiking areas include Rock House, Old Man’s Cave and Ash Cave, with sandstone formations reached from trails.
evidence.quote: The park contains six main hiking areas: Ash Cave, Cantwell Cliffs, Cedar Falls, Old Man's Cave, Rock House and Whispering Cave.

evidence.claim: Seven openings look past stone columns into the forest at Rock House, the only non-recess cave in Hocking Hills State Park.
evidence.quote: This is the only non-recess cave within Hocking Hills State Park, with a main section around 25 feet high, 200 feet long, and 20-30 feet wide. A row of seven openings provide a view past the formation's stone columns and into the surrounding forest.

evidence.claim: Indigenous people used the cave for thousands of years. Tourism followed with the construction of the Rock House Hotel in 1835.
evidence.quote: The cave was used by indigenous people for thousands of years, and the location has been a tourist destination since the construction of the Rock House Hotel in 1835.

evidence.claim: During the Depression, Civilian Conservation Corps Company 526, based at Camp Logan and largely employing Black workers, improved Rock House along with Cantwell Cliffs and Rockbridge.
evidence.quote: Another troop, Company 526, was based at Camp Logan and largely employed Black workers who were twice as likely to suffer from unemployment during the Depression. Workers from Company 526 improved places including the Cantwell Cliffs, Rock House, and Rockbridge sites.

evidence.claim: By the camp’s closure in 1937, Company 526 had also paved miles of roadways and planted 300,000 trees across its work areas.
evidence.quote: By the time of the camp's closure in 1937, Company 526 had built and paved miles of roadways, improved over 2,000 acres of parkland and planted 300,000 trees.

evidence.claim: Look through the row of seven openings past the stone columns toward the forest.
evidence.quote: A row of seven openings provide a view past the formation's stone columns and into the surrounding forest.

evidence.claim: Conkle’s Hollow narrows to 100 feet in places, with cliffs about 200 feet tall above the gorge.
evidence.quote: Conkle's Hollow State Nature Preserve is a deep, cool gorge, which is only 100 feet wide in places and is considered by some to be the deepest in Ohio.  The cliffs above the gorge are about 200 feet tall.

evidence.claim: Ferns, hemlock and wildflowers cover its floor.
evidence.quote: The valley floor is covered in many species of plants, such as ferns, hemlock, and various wildflowers.

evidence.claim: Two trails follow different levels of the hollow: one traces the rim, while the other follows the bottom.
evidence.quote: The hollow features two trails, one rim trail following the upper edge of the gorge and a handicap-accessible trail that follows the gorge bottom.

evidence.claim: Nearby, the preserved main cabin of Camp Hocking marks a Civilian Conservation Corps base. Company 505 worked from this camp on erosion control, trails and stone masonry elsewhere in the Hocking Hills.
evidence.quote: Company 505 was one of the first in Ohio and based at Camp Hocking near Conkles Hollow. This company worked on numerous projects including erosion control, trail construction and maintenance, and stone masonry for newly formed trails in sites like Tar Hollow, Ash Cave, and Old Man's Cave. The main cabin of Camp Hocking has been preserved and is located next to Conkles Hollow.

evidence.claim: Company 505’s projects included Ash Cave and Old Man’s Cave, linking the nearby camp to the trail network beyond this narrow gorge.
evidence.quote: This company worked on numerous projects including erosion control, trail construction and maintenance, and stone masonry for newly formed trails in sites like Tar Hollow, Ash Cave, and Old Man's Cave.

evidence.claim: Ash Cave is a recess worn into sandstone, stretching 700 feet from end to end and rising 90 feet at its highest point.
evidence.quote: Like many of the caves located within the Hocking Hills, Ash Cave is a recess cave formed by the gradual erosion of sandstone over centuries. It measures 700 feet from end-to-end and rises 90 feet tall at its highest point.

evidence.claim: Across the park, groundwater and streams eroded the sandstone over millions of years, producing the rock formations and waterfalls.
evidence.quote: millions of years of groundwater and streams eroded the soft sandstone to form immense rock formations and waterfalls.

evidence.claim: Its name comes from piles of ash that white settlers found on the floor. Archaeologists believe the ashes came from campfires accumulated over centuries of use by Indigenous cultures.
evidence.quote: The cave was named for large piles of ashes that white settlers found on the cave floor when they first visited the site. Archeologists believe these were the remains of campfires that accumulated over centuries of use by indigenous cultures.

evidence.claim: The space has also hosted meetings and worship services, followed by annual summer concerts by the Columbus Symphony Orchestra beginning in 2022.
evidence.quote: In recent years the space has been used to host meetings, worship services, and, since 2022, annual summer concerts by the Columbus Symphony Orchestra.
